question.worked_solution:
First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{{x}^{2}+4x+3} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{{x}^{2}+3x+x+3} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{x(x+3)+1(x+3)} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{(x+1)(x+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that the function has two vertical asymptotes  $x=-1$ and $x=-3.$ 

Since $x=-1$ is a vertical asymptote, the limit as $x\to (-1)^{-}$ will be either $+\infty $ or $-\infty .$

To find the limit as $x\to (-1)^{-},$ we evaluate $f(x)$ at $x$-values very close to $x=-1$ from the left:

| $x$ | $-1.1$ | $-1.01$ | $-1.001$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $≈-23.21$ | $≈-203.02$ | $≈-2\,003.00$ |

All values are negative and get smaller and smaller. Therefore, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x)=-\infty .
$$

This matches up with what we see in the graph of $f(x),$ shown below.
